title: Faith in a World Full of Bait

sections.heading: Seeing the traps for what they are
sections.text:
Lord, this world knows how to make sin look beautiful. It comes dressed up as something harmless, exciting, successful, or satisfying. It holds out shiny bait and gives ugly things a charming face.

Please train my faith to look past the paint and glitter. Help me recognize what would pull me away from you before I reach for it. Keep me from the traps that flatter me, entertain me, or promise life without you. Give me the kind of trust in Christ that does not just notice temptation, but overcomes it.
theological_themes: The world, in its fallen opposition to God, often presents sin as attractive and life-giving.
Faith is not mere optimism; it is trust in Christ that enables discernment and endurance against worldly temptation.

scripture_references.connection: John teaches that faith in Jesus is the means by which believers overcome the world. This directly grounds the prayer’s request for faith that sees through worldly snares and resists them.

This passage warns that the desires and pride bound up with the world are passing away and opposed to love for the Father. It supports the prayer’s concern that attractive things can become spiritually dangerous when they draw the heart from God.

sections.heading: Serving you with active faith and love
sections.text:
In the work you have given me to do, make me steady and willing. Give me energy when I am lazy, courage when I am afraid, and a real devotion to what matters to you.

Let my love be more than a feeling. Make it a working grace in me—something that moves my hands, shapes my choices, and shows up in ordinary obedience. Let my trust in you grow large enough that my life begins to match it.
theological_themes: Faith should express itself in active obedience, courage, perseverance, and love.
Christian love is not passive sentiment but Spirit-shaped action in daily duties.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says that what counts in Christ is faith working through love. This supports the prayer’s movement from inward trust to outward, energetic obedience.

Because Christ is risen and the believer’s labor is not empty, Paul calls Christians to be steadfast and abounding in the Lord’s work. That fits the request for firmness, zeal, and courage in ordinary duties.

sections.heading: Opening the door again to Christ’s nearness
sections.text:
I miss the felt nearness of my Lord. When I am aware of your presence, even ordinary life becomes full of light. Your voice steadies me. Your closeness strengthens every grace in me.

But I admit that my unbelief often shuts the door. I live as if you are distant, as if I must manage life on my own, as if your promises are not solid enough to lean on. Father, give me faith that welcomes Christ again—not as a guest for a moment, but as the One who stays with me and rules my heart.
theological_themes: Believers may lose the felt enjoyment of Christ’s presence through unbelief, even though Christ remains faithful to his own.
Faith welcomes and relies on Christ’s indwelling presence, leading to renewed communion and strength.

scripture_references.connection: Paul prays that believers would be strengthened by the Spirit so that Christ may dwell in their hearts through faith. This closely supports the request that faith would give Christ welcome and room in the heart.
Jesus calls his disciples to abide in him because fruitfulness depends on ongoing communion with him. This grounds the prayer’s longing for Christ’s presence as the source of spiritual strength.

sections.heading: Receiving the riches of your Word by faith
sections.text:
Your Word is full of promises, but I do not want to leave them unopened. By faith, help me gather what you have given there.

Make me rich with its truth, strong with its power, and glad in its joy. Let me stay near its sweetness instead of rushing past it. Feed me through Scripture like bread from heaven, so that my soul gains fresh strength from what you have spoken.
theological_themes: God’s promises in Scripture are spiritually nourishing and strengthening when received by faith.
The Word of God is not merely information; it is a means by which God gives life, joy, wisdom, and endurance.

scripture_references.connection: Peter says God has granted precious and great promises through which believers share in what they need for godliness. This supports the prayer’s desire to become rich and strong through the promises of God.
Jesus teaches that human beings live by every word that comes from God’s mouth. This grounds the prayer’s image of Scripture as soul-sustaining food.
The psalmist describes God’s words as sweet, expressing delight in Scripture rather than bare duty. This illuminates the prayer’s longing to taste and enjoy the sweetness of God’s Word.

sections.heading: Asking for the faith I still lack
sections.text: Lord, increase my faith. Make it clear-eyed, brave, active, and hungry for your Word. Teach me to trust you more deeply than I trust what I can see, feel, buy, control, or prove. Keep me close to Christ, and let my life show that I belong to him. Amen.
theological_themes: Faith itself is a gift believers may ask God to strengthen.
Growing faith reshapes perception, desire, obedience, and perseverance.

scripture_references.connection: The apostles directly ask Jesus to increase their faith. This gives biblical language and warrant for the prayer’s final, simple request.
The father in this account confesses both real faith and remaining unbelief. That tension fits the prayer’s honest dependence on God to strengthen trust where it is weak.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s language about mourning the absence of the beloved Lord could be misunderstood as Christ actually abandoning a believer. I rendered it as the loss of felt nearness and communion, while preserving the seriousness of unbelief.

The line about unbelief keeping Christ outside the door could be read as a conversion appeal or as implying that Christ’s presence depends mechanically on the believer’s performance. I framed it as a relational failure of trust within the believer’s ongoing life with Christ.

The original uses “the world” in the Johannine sense of fallen desires and systems opposed to God, not as contempt for creation itself or ordinary human life. The adaptation keeps that distinction by focusing on sin’s attractive bait rather than on created things as evil in themselves.
significant_interpretive_choices: I kept the original’s concrete imagery of painted, glittering bait because it is central to the prayer’s view of temptation: sin deceives by appearing desirable.
I interpreted “love as a working grace” as love expressed in practical obedience and daily action, supported by Galatians 5:6.

I treated the final request, “Lord, increase my faith,” as the summary of the whole prayer rather than a separate topic: stronger faith discerns temptation, energizes duty, welcomes Christ, and receives Scripture’s promises.
